section.heading: 9.3. Applications of Separable Differential Equations
section.paragraph: In this section, we look at some applications of first-order separable differential equations. We begin by revisiting some of the applications discussed in Section 9.1.
section.heading: Unrestricted Growth Models
section.paragraph: The differential equation describing an unrestricted growth model is given by
$$\frac{\mathit{dQ}}{\mathit{dt}} = kQ$$
where $$Q(t)$$ represents the size of a certain population at time $$t$$ and $$k$$ is a positive constant. Separating the variables in this differential equation and integrating, we have

$$\begin{array}{rcll} {\int\frac{\mathit{dQ}}{Q}} & = & {\int{kdt}} & \\ {\ln|Q|} & = & {kt + C_{1}} & \\ |Q| & = & {e^{kt + C_{1}} = e^{\mathit{kt}}e^{C_{1}} = C_{2}e^{\mathit{kt}}} & { {C_{2} = e^{C_{1}}}} \\ Q & = & \mathit{Ce}^{\mathit{kt}} & { {C = \pm C_{2}}} \end{array}$$
Thus, we may write the solution as
$$Q(t) = \mathit{Ce}^{\mathit{kt}}$$
Observe that if the quantity present initially is denoted by $$Q_{0}$$ , then $$Q(0) = Q_{0}$$ . Applying this condition yields the equation

Therefore, the model for unrestricted exponential growth with initial population $$Q_{0}$$ is given by
$$Q(t) = Q_{0}e^{\mathit{kt}}$$
(Figure 7).

section.heading: Restricted Growth Models
section.paragraph: From Section 9.1, we see that a differential equation describing a restricted growth model is given by
$$\frac{\mathit{dQ}}{\mathit{dt}} = k\left( {C - Q} \right)$$
where both $$k$$ and $$C$$ are positive constants. To solve this separable first-order differential equation, we first separate the variables and then integrate, obtaining

$$\begin{array}{rcll} {\int\frac{\mathit{dQ}}{C - Q}} & = & {\int{kdt}} & \\ {- \ln\left| {C - Q} \right|} & = & {kt + C_{1}} & { {C_{1} \text{, an arbitrary constant} }} \\ {\ln\left| {C - Q} \right|} & = & {- kt - C_{1}} & \\ \left| {C - Q} \right| & = & {e^{- kt - C_{1}} = e^{- kt}e^{- C_{1}} = C_{2}e^{- kt}} & { {C_{2} = e^{- C_{1}}}} \\ {C - Q} & = & \mathit{Ae}^{- kt} & { {A = \pm C_{2}}} \\ Q & = & {C - \mathit{Ae}^{- kt}} & \end{array}$$
This is the equation of the learning curve (Figure 9) studied in Chapter 5.

section.paragraph: Next, let’s consider a differential equation describing another type of restricted growth:
$$\frac{\mathit{dQ}}{\mathit{dt}} = kQ\left( {C - Q} \right)$$
where $$k$$ and $$C$$ are positive constants. Separating variables and integrating each side of the resulting equation with respect to the appropriate variable, we have
$$\int\frac{1}{Q(C - Q)}dQ\int kdt$$
As it stands, the integrand on the left side of this equation is not in a form that can be easily integrated. However, observe that
$$\frac{1}{Q\left( {C - Q} \right)} = \frac{1}{C}\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{Q} + \frac{1}{C - Q}} \right\rbrack$$
as you may verify by adding the terms between the brackets on the right-hand side. Making use of this identity, we have

$$\begin{array}{rcl} {\int{\frac{1}{C}\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{Q} + \frac{1}{C - Q}} \right\rbrack dQ}} & = & {\int{kdt}} \\ {\int{\frac{\mathit{dQ}}{Q} + {\int\frac{\mathit{dQ}}{C - Q}}}} & = & {Ck{\int\mathit{dt}}} \\ {\ln|Q| - \ln\left| {C - Q} \right|} & = & {{Ckt + b} {b, \text{an arbitrary} {constant}}} \\ {\ln\left| \frac{Q}{C - Q} \right|} & = & {Ckt + b} \\ \left| \frac{Q}{C - Q} \right| & = & {e^{Ckt + b} = e^{b}e^{Ckt}} \\ \frac{Q}{C - Q} & = & {\mathit{Be}^{Ckt} {B = \pm e^{b}}} \\ Q & = & {\mathit{CBe}^{Ckt} - \mathit{QBe}^{Ckt}} \\ {{({1 + \mathit{Be}^{Ckt}})}Q} & = & \mathit{CBe}^{Ckt} \end{array}$$
and
$$Q = \frac{\mathit{CBe}^{Ckt}}{1 + \mathit{Be}^{Ckt}}$$
or
$${Q(t) = \frac{C}{1 + \mathit{Ae}^{- Ckt}}} {A = \frac{1}{B}}$$
(see Figure 2). In its final form, this function is equivalent to the logistic function encountered in Chapter 5.

section.heading: 9.3. Concept Questions

list.item: 1. Consider the differential equation $$\frac{\mathit{dQ}}{\mathit{dt}} = kQ\left( {k > 0} \right)$$ describing unrestricted growth. Assume that $$Q(0) = Q_{0} > 0$$ . What does the equation say about the rate of growth of $$Q$$ with respect to $$t$$ ? What happens to the rate of growth as $$t$$ approaches infinity? Reconcile your answer to part (a) with the solution $$Q(t) = Q_{0}e^{\mathit{kt}}$$ of the differential equation.

2. Consider the differential equation $$\frac{\mathit{dR}}{\mathit{dS}} = \frac{k}{S}\left( {k > 0} \right)$$ describing the relationship between a stimulus $$S$$ and the resulting response $$R$$ (the Weber–Fechner Law). What can you say about the rate of change of $$R$$ with respect to $$S$$ ? What happens to the rate of change as $$S$$ approaches infinity? Reconcile your answers to part (a) with the solution $$R = k\ln\frac{S}{S_{0}}$$ of the differential equation. Assume that $$S(0) = S_{0} > 0$$ .
